M0037:
# M0037

If you get this error then you are trying to message from a
block or expression that has no send capability, such as the
top level of an `actor`.

You can also get this error when you are trying to message or
`throw` an error from the `finally` clause of a `try` block.

`finally` clauses are generally used to clean up local state
in the event of messaging failures, and are especially invoked when
the processing of an `await` result traps. In this last-resort cleanup
only local manipulations are allowed to (e.g.) release locks and thus
prevent the canister from ending up in a stuck state.

Should you encounter this error, so make sure that you move all messaging
code out of the `finally` block. In all other cases where send capability
is available, wrapping the indicated expression in an `async` can help.
M0003:
# M0003

This error means that a module tried to import itself.

Erroneous code example (file is called `Self.mo`):

```motoko
import S "./Self"; // import error, file Self.mo must not depend on itself

module { ... }
```

If you encounter this error you should probably remove the offending import.
M0149:
# M0149

This error means that you supplied an immutable record field (declared without `var`), where a mutable record field (specified with `var`), was expected.

Erroneous code example:

```motoko
{ count = 0 } : { var count : Nat }
```

If you encounter this error, you should probably insert the `var` keyword:

```motoko
{ var count = 1 } : { var count : Nat }
```
M0150:
# M0150

This error means you supplied a mutable record field (declared with `var`) where an immutable record field (specified without `var`) was expected.

Erroneous code example:

```motoko
{ var name = "Fred" } : { name : Text }
```

If you encounter this error, you should probably omit `var`:

```motoko
{ name = "Fred" } : { name : Text }
```
M0153:
# M0153

This error means that an imported Candid file (`.did`) mentions types that
cannot be represented in Motoko. These are

* `float32`
* `service` types with method names that are not identifiers, e.g. because
  they contain special characters.

If you encounter this error, and you can, you should avoid these types in the
service’s interface. If you have no control over the interface, you cannot
interact with it from Motoko.
M0156:
# M0156

This error means that a parameterized type definition, or set of type definitions, is too complicated for Motoko to accept.

Motoko rejects type definitions that are expansive, in the sense that unfolding type definitions may produce an ever-expanding set of types.

For example, the type definition:

```motoko
type List<T> = ?(T, List<T>);
```

that recursively instantiates `List` at the same parameter `T`, is non-expansive and accepted, but the similar looking definition:

```motoko
type Seq<T> = ?(T, Seq<[T]>);
```

that recursively instantiates `Seq` with a larger type, `[T]`, containing `T`, is *expansive* and rejected.

If you encounter this error, try to restructure your type definitions to be non-expansive.
M0185:
# M0185

This warning means that an imported Candid file (`.did`) describes a service
constructor rather than a service: its `service` takes initialization
arguments, which a canister receives once, when it is installed.

Example of such a Candid file, as generated for an actor class:

```candid
service : (owner : principal) -> {
  greet : (text) -> (text);
}
```

Importing it, e.g. with `import Backend "canister:backend"`, gives you the
canister as the service it creates, as if the file read

```candid
service : {
  greet : (text) -> (text);
}
```

The initialization arguments are ignored. They do not matter for calling the
methods of an installed canister, so if that is all you do, the warning is
harmless.

If you wrote the Candid file by hand, you can avoid the warning by removing the
initialization arguments, as in the second example above. If the file is
generated for a canister, e.g. for a `canister:` import, leave it as it is;
the warning only tells you that the arguments are not part of the import.
M0158:
# M0158

This error means that you declared a public class without providing it with a name.

Erroneous code example:

```motoko
public class () {};
```

If you encounter this error, you should probably name the class or make it private.

```motoko
public class C() {};
```

Public fields must be named since they determine the interface of the enclosing object.
M0195:
# M0195

This warning means that you called a function that demands elevated (`system`) capabilities,
without manifestly passing the capability.
M0197:
# M0197

This error means that you tried to call a function that requires (`system`) capabilities,
in a context that does not provide them.

Only actor bodies, async expressions, non-query async function bodies and
local functions with a leading `system` type parameter have system capabilities.
M0212:
# M0212

This warning means that you are affixing a parenthetical note to a message send (i.e. either
a canister method call of a self-send with `async`, or `actor`) that contains an attribute not recognised
by this version of the Motoko compiler.

Currently, only these attributes are recognized in parenthetical notes:

For _message_ sends and `async` expressions
- `cycles : Nat`
- `timeout : Nat32`

For `actor` and `actor  class` declarations:
- `migration : {<old-fields>} -> {<current-fields>}`
M0274:
# M0274

This error means that a reserved keyword of the Motoko language (such as
`query`, `stable`, `implicit`, or `in`) was used where an identifier is
expected, for example as a variable, field, or function name.

Keywords cannot be used as identifiers. Choose a different name, for example
by appending an underscore:

```motoko
let query_ = 5;      // not: let query = 5
```
M0275:
# M0275

This error means that the branches of an `if` (or the body of a `while` or
`for`) were written as bare expressions while the condition or head is an
unparenthesized compound expression: a call, an indexing, a projection, or an
operator application.

When the head is written without parentheses, the branches or body must be
blocks:

```motoko
if f(x) { e1 } else { e2 };   // not: if f(x) e1 else e2
while n > 0 { n -= 1 };       // not: while n > 0 n -= 1
for x in xs.vals() { go(x) };
```

Alternatively, keep the branches bare and parenthesize the condition, in the
pre-existing style:

```motoko
if (f(x)) e1 else e2;
```

Whether a `(` or `[` directly after a bare identifier still belongs to the
condition is decided by whitespace: `if c[i] ...` indexes `c`, so its branches
must be blocks, while `if c [i] else []` is the condition `c` followed by the
bare branch `[i]`. A prefix-shaped operator after the condition always starts
the branch: `if (c) -1 else 1`, `if (c) ^mask else mask`, and
`if (c) #less else #greater` keep their meaning, while `if n - 1 > 0 { }` and
`if n-1 > 0 { }` are conditions.

The same error is reported when the body of a `switch` or `do` is not a block,
as in `switch (x) e` or `do e`: these constructs always take a block.
M0276:
# M0276

This error means that a comparison always has the same result, because it is performed at a type that has exactly one value, such as `Any`, `{}`, `()` or `Null`.
A comparison at such a type cannot observe any difference between its operands.

The error is reported only when that type was not written for both operands: their types differ, and their common supertype is the single-valued type, a type parameter is compared at its bound, or a literal is compared with a value of type `Any`, as in `x == 10`.

This is almost always a mistake, such as comparing the wrong variables, or two records that share no field:

```motoko
let n : Nat = 1;
let t : Text = "1";
n == t; // compared at `Any`

let user = { id = 1; name = "Ann" };
let order = { userId = 1; total = 10 };
user == order; // compared at `{}`

func eq<A, B>(a : A, b : B) : Bool = a == b; // compared at `Any`
```

Compare the fields you mean explicitly, or convert the operands to a common type first:

```motoko
user.id == order.userId;
Nat.toText(n) == t;
```

For generic code, take an equality function as a parameter instead:

```motoko
func eq<A>(a : A, b : A, equal : (A, A) -> Bool) : Bool = equal(a, b);
```

When both operands already have the single-valued type, the comparison is accepted, because the type was declared that way on purpose:

```motoko
type Admin = { status : { #active } };
func isActive(a : Admin) : Bool = a.status == #active; // always `true`, but accepted
```

If the constant result is really intended in the other cases, `-W M0276` reports this as a warning instead of an error.
M0277:
# M0277

This error means that the body of a function spells out the `async` that its return type already implies.

The body of a function returning `async T` is implicitly asynchronous, whether it is written as a block or as `= <exp>`:

```motoko
func fetch() : async Nat = async { 42 }; // the body would be `async { async { 42 } }`
```

Write the body without `async`:

```motoko
func fetch() : async Nat { 42 };
func fetch2() : async Nat = 42; // the same
```

The same holds for `async*`, and for a one-way `shared` function, returning `()`, whose body is implicitly `ignore async`:

```motoko
public func notify() : () = ignore (async { log("hi") }); // a second message
public func notify() : () { log("hi") };
```

A parenthetical on the body, as in `= (with cycles = 1_000) async { ... }`, belongs where the function is called instead: `(with cycles = 1_000) fetch()`.
